venue_now: arXiv preprint 2504.16074v2, 18 May 2025, marked 'Preprint. Under review.' (p. 1); the text shows no venue
what_it_is: A benchmark of 500 text-only physics problems, from high-school exercises to Physics Olympiad level, adapted from exercises for human learners by 178 Peking University physics students and filtered through expert review and a test by 81 students, which kept 500 of 757 questions (p. 1, p. 4, p. 5). Each problem asks for a single symbolic expression for a target quantity (p. 3-4); answers are scored by binary equivalence and by the EED Score, a partial-credit tree edit distance between the SymPy expression trees of the model's and the reference answer (p. 5-6). The best model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 36.9% accuracy against a 61.9% human baseline (p. 1, p. 6). The paper adds a manual first-error analysis of model traces and a chain-of-thought poisoning test (p. 8-9), but scores only the final expression (p. 10, p. 20).
domain: physics, high school to Physics Olympiad: mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, optics, modern physics and advanced physics (p. 2-3)
size: 500 problems retained from 757 (p. 5); 16 models (14 by API, 2 locally), shown in 19 configurations in Figure 1 (p. 2, p. 6); human baseline from 81 students, 559 valid answer sheets (p. 6)
source_of_items: adapted from physics exercises designed for human learners, from non-public and public sources 'none of which are easily discoverable through direct internet search', by 178 students of the PKU School of Physics; reviewed by experts with LLM outputs shown to flag ambiguity (p. 4-5)
has_gold_traces: partial: human reference solutions exist (a full solution averages about 3,000 characters, p. 27) and one is truncated for the chain-of-thought poisoning test (p. 27, p. 30), but scoring uses only the final expression (p. 5-6; the authors say so, p. 10, p. 20)
evaluation: final answer, expression-level: binary accuracy (symbolic equivalence) and the EED Score (100 for an exact match, 60 - 100r for relative tree edit distance 0 < r < 0.6, else 0), computed on SymPy expression trees with subtree operations (p. 5-6); answers extracted from a boxed LaTeX expression (p. 23)
human_validation: Items: drafted and adapted by 178 students (p. 4); each question checked by expert reviewers against the construction rules, with o1 and DeepSeek-R1 outputs displayed to expose ambiguity (p. 5); 81 students, 50 of them at Chinese Physics Olympiad gold-medal level, attempted subsets and reported clarity and uniqueness problems, after which 500 of 757 questions were kept (p. 5). The same students give the human baseline, 61.9 +/- 2.1% accuracy and EED 70.4 +/- 1.8 (p. 6). The EED metric is supported by bootstrap sample-efficiency and parameter-robustness analyses (p. 6-7), not by comparison with human grading.
contamination_measures: original or adapted problems from sources not easily found by web search (p. 4); the test-time-scaling comparison uses 'the open source 100 questions' (p. 23), which suggests that only part of the 500 is public, though the paper describes no held-out split

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: 'Symbolic' fits the answer format: each answer must be a single symbolic expression, with equations and floating-point approximations rejected (p. 4), and it is scored by expression-tree edit distance (p. 5-6). 'Advanced' is loose: difficulty runs from high-school exercises to Olympiad problems (p. 1, p. 4). The benchmark's stated target is physical perception and multi-step reasoning in 'realistic physical scenarios' (title; p. 4), and its own error analysis puts most failures in deriving new equations from the physical situation rather than in symbolic manipulation (p. 8; Table 2, p. 9), so 'targets symbolic understanding' describes the format rather than the aim. S-P2: physics only, with no engineering context, is fair for this paper; 'theoretical physics' is loose for exercise-style problems set in realistic scenarios (p. 4).

suggested_wording: PHYBench (Qiu et al., 2025) requires a single symbolic expression for each of 500 curated problems from high-school to Olympiad level and grades it by expression-tree edit distance, which by its authors' account scores the final expression and not the reasoning that produced it.
facts_to_cite: 500 text-only physics problems from high-school to Physics Olympiad difficulty, covering mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, optics, modern and advanced physics (p. 1, p. 3, p. 4).

Problems were adapted from exercises designed for human learners, from non-public and public sources, by 178 Peking University physics students (p. 4); 500 of 757 reviewed questions were kept after a test by 81 students (p. 5).
Each answer must be a single symbolic expression; equations and floating-point approximations are rejected (p. 4).

Answers are scored by accuracy and by the EED Score, a partial-credit tree edit distance between SymPy expression trees (p. 5-6); on 500 problems EED gives the discriminative power of about 1,500 problems scored by accuracy, a 204% sample-efficiency gain (p. 1, p. 6, p. 7).
The best model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 36.9% accuracy and EED 49.5; 81 students (50 at Chinese Physics Olympiad gold-medal level) reach 61.9 +/- 2.1% (p. 1, p. 6).

The authors state that the EED Score focuses on final answer quality and 'does not capture the full reasoning process', and that process-level evaluation is costly to scale and complicated by non-unique solution paths (p. 10, p. 20).

A manual analysis of the first mistake in traces from seven models on 50 problems finds that typically more than 90% of errors arise in reasoning rather than in perceiving the physical situation, and over 90% of those in deriving new equations rather than manipulating them (p. 8; Table 2, p. 9).

A chain-of-thought poisoning test injects one of six perturbations into a truncated reference solution and checks whether the model detects or propagates the error (p. 8-9, p. 27); the appendix illustrates the protocol on one problem (Problem 719, p. 30).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: long multi-step derivations in realistic physical scenarios (p. 4); human reference solutions (p. 27); a manual first-error analysis of model traces (p. 8) and an injected-error test on a truncated reference solution (p. 8-9, p. 27-30), which resemble EngTrace's step labels and planted defects but probe the solver, not an evaluator; a human baseline. Lacks: generated instances (500 fixed problems); step-level or process evaluation (EED scores the final expression only, and the authors defer process evaluation, p. 10, p. 20); numeric answers (symbolic only, p. 4); an engineering setting; validation of the grader against expert judgement. Its stated obstacle to process scoring, non-unique solution paths (p. 20), bears directly on EngTrace's choice to check intermediate values order-free rather than a canonical step sequence (state brief section 2).
notes: 'Original' in the abstract (p. 1) means adapted from existing exercises and curated (p. 4), not newly authored, so the revised text should say 'curated' or 'adapted'. The public release may be 100 of the 500 problems (p. 23); the paper does not say how the rest are held. The May reference list misprints all three printed given names (citation_context_map.md). Its limitation statement (p. 10, p. 20) is citable in the planned process-supervision paragraph as an explicit example of a physics benchmark that leaves the reasoning process unscored. For this paper alone, 'scores only the final answer (expression)' would be accurate.
